#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when the version you get isn't the one you chose*
This scenario demonstrates the "diamond dependency" problem, where two paths through the graph request different versions of the same library.

It highlights the fundamental difference in resolution strategy between Maven ("nearest wins") and Gradle/sbt ("highest wins").

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
Depth ties broken by declaration order applies since **Maven 2.0.9**.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:2.0.0]
    Root --> LibB_Direct[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB_Transitive[lib-b:2.0.0]
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s2-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
The newer version (`2.0.0`) wins so that `lib-a` gets the API it was built against, or the direct dependency (`1.0.0`) wins because it was explicitly requested.

#### ! Actual
Resolves `lib-b:1.0.0`. The direct declaration is at depth 1; `lib-a`'s request is at depth 2. Nearest wins.

*   **Maven**: `lib-b-1.0.0.jar` is on the classpath. `lib-a` may crash if it uses API that only exists in `2.0.0`.
*   **Gradle/sbt**: `lib-b-2.0.0.jar` is on the classpath. Your own code may crash if it uses API removed in `2.0.0`.

#### ! Why
Maven assumes the declaration closest to the root is the intentional one: you wrote it, so you meant it. When two candidates sit at the same depth, the one declared **first** in the POM wins, which makes the order of `<dependency>` blocks significant and easy to break by accident. Gradle and sbt instead assume the highest version is the safest, on the semver bet that newer versions are backward compatible.

#### ! Fix
*   **Manage the version:** put `lib-b` in `<dependencyManagement>` at the version you have tested. This decides the conflict regardless of depth ([MS6](../scenario-6-forcing/guide.qmd)).
*   **Align the direct declaration:** if `lib-a` genuinely needs `2.0.0`, change your direct `lib-b` to `2.0.0` and test your own code against it.
*   **Reorder declarations:** only relevant for equal-depth ties, and fragile. Do not rely on it.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Pinning via `<dependencyManagement>` to a version both consumers were tested with.
* MEDIUM Adding a direct declaration just to shorten the distance; it works, but the reason is invisible to the next reader.
* HIGH Reordering `<dependency>` blocks to flip a tie-break. It is fragile, undocumented in the POM, and widely misunderstood.

#### ! Control
Use `<dependencyManagement>` to fix the version regardless of depth. Gradle uses `constraints` or `platform` (BOM) for similar control; sbt uses `dependencyOverrides`.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose`

**What to look for:** Lines containing `omitted for conflict with 1.0.0` under `lib-a`. (Gradle prints `2.0.0 -> 1.0.0 (by conflict resolution)`; sbt reports an eviction.)

**Conclusion:** The winning version is the one nearest the root, not necessarily the newest or the most compatible.

#### ! Scales
This is the primary cause of "dependency hell". As graphs grow, "nearest" becomes arbitrary and "newest" can trigger unintended upgrades.

#### ! Takeaway
Maven optimises for distance; Gradle and sbt optimise for freshness. Knowing which strategy your tool uses is the first thing to check when a version is not the one you expected.

#### ! Wild

In 2015, a [remote code execution vulnerability in Apache Commons Collections](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fjq5-5j5f-mvxh) (CVE-2015-7501) affected a large part of the Java ecosystem. The vulnerable library was embedded deep in the transitive dependency graphs of [IBM WebSphere, Oracle WebLogic, and Red Hat JBoss](https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/986a8488-052e-46d1-8ede-c55cbfceb822), application servers widely deployed in financial services and government.

Many organisations couldn't upgrade the affected application server or vendor SDK directly. Maven's "nearest wins" logic often favoured the older, vulnerable version (being slightly "closer" to the root). The practical fix was `<dependencyManagement>` to pin the patched Commons Collections version globally, satisfying security audits without requiring full regression testing of the vendor stack.
